title: Primitive element for finite fields
note: Reproduces exactly, and one line explains both halves -- but the overwrite is deliberate, not an oversight. galois.m2:173-178: 'if d >= opts.SizeLimit or primitiveElement != S_0 then (typ = "FlintBig"; primitiveElement = S_0; -- Possibly NOT the primitive element in this case!!'. In the reported ring d = 48 < SizeLimit = 10000, so the trigger is the second disjunct, which fires whenever the primitive element is not the ring's own variable, discarding both FindOne's search (galois.m2:156-161) and the user's argument before galois.m2:200 stores the result as F.PrimitiveElement. Control: in ZZ/7[z]/(z^2-z-3) isPrimitive z is false (order 24 of 48) and F.PrimitiveElement comes back z; in ZZ/7[w]/(w^2-w+3) isPrimitive w is true and F.PrimitiveElement is correctly w; the rings differ in nothing else. Scope of the damage, measured: the substitution exists so ringmap.m2:122/133/142 can tell the engine where S_0 goes rather than where a primitive element goes, and it works -- 200 random pairs through map(F[t], F) on both the FlintBig and Zech paths gave zero additive or multiplicative failures. So arithmetic and ring maps are sound and only the option and the exposed attribute are wrong. The documentation demonstrates the broken usage: ov_rings.m2:644-648 promises 'your own choice of primitive element', says elements are stored internally as powers of it, and shows GF(ZZ/2[T]/(T^9+T+1), PrimitiveElement => T^3+1) -- T^3+1 has order 511, T does not, 511 < SizeLimit, and k.PrimitiveElement returns T. note: The reported difference is deliberate on both sides, and the reason QQ[x] differs from the other three rings is not the one given in the thread. gcd(QQ,QQ) never reaches the engine at all: m2/integers.m2:51-53 defines it as a rational content gcd -- clear both denominators to a common d, take the integer gcd of the numerators, divide back -- so gcd(2_QQ,4_QQ) is 2. There is no TypeFamily and no UnionType in m2/ or d/ -- the only hit for the latter is the unrelated ffiUnionType in d/ffi.d:609 -- and Number is a plain Type with InfiniteNumber and IndeterminateNumber as ordinary subtypes (m2/max.m2:6,18), not a union of ZZ, QQ, RR and friends. author: mahrud
title: Feature request: {1..5} as syntax for toList(1..5)
note: Unimplemented and unresolved. Replay confirms {1..5} still gives {(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)}, and [1..5] and <|1..5|> likewise. The 26-comment thread is a disagreement rather than a plan: Dan opened with 'that is more intuitive syntax, good idea' and pointed at convertr.d, then argued the change makes the language more complicated, floated a three-period operator to distinguish it from the binary one, and offered the existing spelling splice {1..3, 4, 2:5}; mahrud showed splice does not scale, since splice {(0,0)..(1,1), (2,2), 2:(3,3)} flattens the pairs too; pzinn objected that {1..5} should logically hold a sequence; Mike noted he and Dan had tried years ago to make 1..n and r:1 part of lists and could not find a good way. Dan's one concession, 'making {1..5} expand to {1,2,3,4,5} at parsing time is fine', and mahrud's List-versus-Sequence proposal were never taken up. Related: #2020, and #1904, which mahrud wanted to combine with this and which is now implemented.

author: d-torrance
title: monomial exponent overflow: pos int32_t + pos int32_t
note: Reproduces, third-party confirmed 15 days before this triage -- and the fix written for it does not work. State of the three root causes in the diagnosis Doug posted on 2026-05-21. Root cause 1, the C++ exception escaping uncaught through the D interpreter, WAS implemented: 1fcecd4c5f (ddale27, 2026-05-21) wraps every RingElement arithmetic operator in e/ring-elements/ring-element.cpp -- unary minus, +, -, *, *(int), /, power(int), power(mpz_srcptr) -- in try/catch on exc::engine_error, and it shipped in PR #4361, titled 'Fix for the d interface problem in Issue 1984', merged 2026-06-09 and released in 1.26.06. It did not fix the crash. joel-dodge's cmake-macos-15-brew-clang job of 2026-08-04 (run 30943233671, job 92106772709) still shows 'libc++abi: terminating due to uncaught exception of type exc::overflow_exception: monomial exponent overflow: pos int32_t + pos int32_t' at 'capturing check(2, "SuperLinearAlgebra")'. The comparison is valid: that job built 259d30c7ee and 'git merge-base --is-ancestor 1fcecd4c5f 259d30c7ee' succeeds, so the guard was compiled in. So the throw escapes by some route other than RingElement's operators. Monoid::mult (e/monoid.cpp:363, safe::pos_add at :372) is called from many places that are not element arithmetic -- schreyer-orders.cpp, gbring.cpp, res-a0-poly.cpp, Eschreyer.cpp -- and this thread's own 2022-02-10 backtrace reaches Monoid::Monoid via IM2_Monoid_make, i.e. monoid construction. Root causes 2 and 3, both package-level, were never touched: SuperLinearAlgebra.m2:50 still builds a length-2n weight vector for an n-variable ring, so the Weights block is truncated to n zeros and the intended weights are discarded, and check(2)/check(3) still nest superRing over R rather than QQ. The reference build hides this: three 'no-check-flag #1984' markers at lines 225, 263 and 313 of the installed SuperLinearAlgebra.m2 are Debian/PPA patches, not upstream, so check here skips the failing tests. Mike said on 2026-05-21 that he would take a look.

note: Reproduces exactly: kernel f = ideal() while f(u-v) = 0, on F = frac(QQ[u]), R1 = F[], R2 = F[v], f = map(R1,R2,{u}). Root cause was diagnosed in-thread by jieaosong in 2021 and never acted on: kernel uses selectInSubring(1, ...) on the graph ring (m2/ringmap.m2), but with no variables in R1 the Eliminate 0 block is indistinguishable from the default order, because empty blocks are elided in the engine at e/interface/monomial-ordering.cpp by 'return (p->nvars > 0);' -- so selectInSubring counts blocks wrongly and eliminates the wrong one. author: matthias314
title: `rank` is very slow for some matrices
note: Reproduces, and the number is worse than 'slow': measured on the reporter's own attachment (rankbug.txt, a 32x32 matrix over ZZ/2 in 5 variables), rank transpose M takes 0.0026 s and rank M takes 69.4 s. Both return 32. That is a factor of 27000 for the same mathematical quantity, and the control is exact rather than approximate, because rank is transpose-invariant and the transpose is the only difference between the two calls -- so this is not a performance wish but a degenerate case in one orientation. kschwede measured 56 s against 0.0025 s in 2021, so nothing has improved in four years. His observation that transposing sometimes helps enormously, with no way to predict which matrices, is the substance of the row and is unaddressed; his det timings (0.85 s dense, 1.97 s with Strategy => Cofactor) show the determinant of the same matrix is cheap, which makes a 69 s rank harder to excuse. matthias314's question, 'Is this a bug?', has never been answered, and his second attachment was 692 s against 76 ms in Sage. mahrud's guess in the thread, that Sage may use Flint where M2 uses fflas_ffpack, was never confirmed by Mike or anyone else.

author: mahrud
title: Heft vector of local rings and Cox rings causes strange betti tables
note: Reproduces exactly on both halves. Over a local ring the Betti tally loses its total degrees: the global kk[u,v] case gives keys (0,{0},0), (1,{2},2), (2,{3},3) while the localization at (u,v) gives (0,{0},0), (1,{2},0), (2,{3},0) -- the third slot, the weight, is 0 throughout -- and heft of the local ring is null, which is mahrud's diagnosis. Passing Weights => {1,1} still fixes the display. ggsmith's answer is the substantive obstacle and it is not a defect claim: for grading groups of rank above one there is no widely agreed weight vector, and computing a good default, such as a minimal ample line bundle on a smooth toric variety, can be prohibitive when the Picard rank is large. So the local-ring half looks fixable -- heft null is a missing default, not a mathematical open question -- while the Cox ring half is genuinely unsettled. Related and newer: #2327 on betti with degree 0 variables, #2303 on BettiTally consistency under nonstandard gradings.

author: DanGrayson
title: curious behavior of "intersect"
note: Reproduces, and both participants are right about different things, which is why it never resolved. The value is commutative and the class is not: intersect(monomialIdeal(x*y^2), ideal(x^2*y)) has class MonomialIdeal, intersect(ideal(x^2*y), monomialIdeal(x*y^2)) has class Ideal, and the two are == as ideals. mahrud's position is that preserving the first argument's type is intended and speeds up algorithms in Saturation; Dan's is that an intersection operator whose result type depends on argument order is not commutative. Neither is contradicted by the other. Related: #1589 on removing MonomialIdeal from the top level, which would dissolve the question, and #4500, ours, on monomialIdeal {} error messages.

author: d-torrance
title: zgesvd did not converge during check(8, "NumericalImplicitization") on armhf
note: Untestable on armhf here, but two things are established. (1) The failing SVD is purely advisory. The message comes from cond_number_via_svd at e/NAG/NAG.cpp:1269, called at :1933 from the path tracker to fill t_s->cond, the condition number of the Jacobian along the homotopy path; that field is written there and read only at :2154 by getSolutionRcond, which hands it to M2 as a solution attribute. It gates no decision in the tracker. Yet on info > 0 the function calls ERROR("zgesvd did not converge") and the whole computation aborts -- a diagnostic that cannot be computed is treated as fatal. The non-fatal pattern is three lines above the call: 'if (!LAPACK_success) t_s->status = SINGULAR;', so the tracker already records LAPACK trouble as a solution status rather than an error. (2) The test passes on amd64: the installed marker is '-- no-check-flag #2183', which captureTestResult honours on every architecture, so it is skipped here too, and extracting the body and running it directly passes. IMPORTANT -- do not read that broad skip as a judgement about scope. Doug explained the history: he skipped everything when he began writing these Debian patches, added the no-check-architecture mechanism later, and never went back to narrow the old ones. Measured: his packaging carries 17 blanket no-check-flag entries against 14 granular ones, with the blanket set skewing old (13 of 17 under #2400) and the granular set carrying the newer numbers. So the marker says when it was written, not where the test fails. Recorded in README.md. Doug's own remark -- never seen on armhf PPA builds or his Raspberry Pi, only the Debian armhf builder -- plus #2230, a LAPACK 3.10.0 assertion in check(4) of this same package, still points at the BLAS/LAPACK implementation rather than at armhf as an instruction set; a sweep of test 8 across six LAPACK implementations on amd64 was run to test that and is reported separately. LAPACK SWEEP, at Doug's request: not supported on amd64. Ran test 8's body under six implementations x 20 seeds via LD_PRELOAD -- reference LAPACK 3.12, ATLAS, OpenBLAS serial/pthread/openmp, and MKL -- and all 120 runs passed with zero zgesvd non-convergences. The control that makes this meaningful: LD_DEBUG=bindings confirms M2-binary binds zgesvd_ to the preloaded library (e.g. atlas/liblapack.so.3), so the swapped implementation really was being called; the binding appears once because lazy binding resolves it once and later calls go via the PLT. This is the weak direction, as flagged before running it: it rules out 'any LAPACK will do this anywhere' but leaves armhf's own floating point, or that one Debian armhf builder, possibly combined with whichever LAPACK it links -- none of which is testable here. Which is why the advisory-SVD finding above is the actionable one: recording a status instead of calling ERROR makes the failure non-fatal on every architecture regardless of what stalls zgesvd.

author: MichaelABurr
title: forceGB and partial/incremental Groebner bases
note: Unmet, in both the general and the specific form. gb.m2:438-446 defines forceGB as a method with only a forceGB Matrix overload, so the forceGB(Matrix,Matrix) that Dan proposed in the Google-group comment MichaelABurr quoted -- asserting that one matrix is a Groebner basis for another -- does not exist; nor does the other half of that comment, that 'gens G' should know G is its own Groebner basis. The underlying ask, feeding partial or degree-limited Groebner information into a later computation, has nothing implementing it. The motivation is concrete and still live: SubalgebraBases computes many nearly identical partial bases and discards the information between them. Closely related and also open: #686, kernel of a ring map should remember its Groebner basis, and #996, the ideal of a Groebner basis should remember it has one -- all three are the same 'do not throw away what we just computed' complaint from different directions.

author: d-torrance
title: assertion failing in check(4, "NumericalImplicitization") with LAPACK 3.10.0
note: Reproduces per the record, and this row already carries a comment from this project posted in the bugs/ phase under the marker bug-triage:bugs/anton/NumericalAG/parallelNumericalImplicitization.m2, so no further comment is proposed. That comment establishes the split: the pasted transcript in that bugs/ file failed with 'degree list should be of length 6' during parallel tracking, which is #3239 and was closed as fixed in #4378, and that error no longer occurs; the wrong image degree is what remains. Worth passing to Doug for packaging rather than for the issue: since #3239 is fixed, the '-- no-check-flag #3239' marker still in the installed NumericalImplicitization/tests.m2 is now obsolete and could come off. Sibling row: #2183, the zgesvd non-convergence in check(8) of this same package, where a sweep of six LAPACK implementations on amd64 found nothing -- so a shared LAPACK explanation for the pair is not supported from this architecture.

author: mikestillman
title: degrees ring not being cached appropriately
note: Reproduces exactly: with R = ZZ/101[a], degreesRing R === degreesRing 1 is false. Dan agreed in one line that they should be the same and nothing followed; two comments in four years, both from 2021-09-08. Mike filed it as a caching problem, which the title still says, and that reading looks right -- the two calls are constructing separate rings rather than returning one cached object, which is the same shape as #2133 in the previous batch, where flattenRing caches for the GaloisField overload at newring.m2:201 and not for the general one at :195. Note for anyone testing this: == is not defined on rings, so the comparison has to be ===.

author: pzinn
title: Proposal: retire PrintNames and PrintNet
note: Unmet: PrintNames and PrintNet are both still in the tree and still referenced from d/binding.d, d/hashtables.dd, m2/max.m2, m2/nets.m2, m2/reals.m2, m2/debugging.m2, m2/packages.m2, m2/remember.m2, m2/robust.m2 and m2/startup.m2.in. Zero comments in four years, so pzinn's three arguments stand unanswered: that the infinite-number case would be simpler without them, that they single out toString and net while leaving html and texMath unable to render CC' properly, and that the texMath mechanism -- a symbol texMath key in the hash table, as CC.texMath already uses -- is the existing general answer. His closing aside is also unresolved and is a separate small bug: he suspects ReverseDictionary and RawMatrix are switched in the code, since RawMatrix appears as an attribute of ReverseDictionary.

author: DanGrayson
title: DegreeRank and degreeLength
note: Unresolved, and the interesting part is that the alternative already exists. DegreeRank is still an option -- 23 mentions in m2/monoids.m2 -- and so is DegreeGroup, with 15 mentions in the same file, so mahrud's 2024-11-18 suggestion to deprecate DegreeRank => n in favour of DegreeGroup => ZZ^n needs no new machinery, only a decision. The naming question Dan actually asked was settled in the thread and never acted on: he asked which Mike preferred and reported on 2021-10-05 that 'Mike likes degree length better'. mahrud's own closing line, 'or maybe we should just leave them both be', is where it stopped. Related: #1312, which mahrud says already carries this conversation, #3007 on degreeLength of a ZZ module, which he argues is unrelated because it concerns engine representation of free modules, and #2239, degreeLength of basic engine rings, filed by Dan the same day as this one.

author: DanGrayson
title: flint pseudoprimality test documentation
note: Narrowed at Doug's direction, and my first note had it wrong. I had written that version#"flint version" supplies the version half of Dan's request and only the documentation fails to surface it. That does not work: documentation is built once and mostly read on the website, so a version baked into the docs records the flint on the BUILD machine, not the reader's -- this machine has flint 3.0.1, and a website build would name whatever it had. version#"flint version", present since Dan's own 35b69aecd6 of 2011-09-21, is the right home for that and already is it. So the version half is dropped and the row is the ALGORITHM half only. That half is unmet and now cheap to settle, because the call chain is short and fully identified: isPseudoprime ZZ at m2/integers.m2:85 calls rawZZisProbablePrime, which is d/interface.dd:4533 into e/interface/flint.cpp:31-39, which calls fmpz_is_probabprime. The doc says only 'This function calls a function in the FLINT library', naming neither the function nor the algorithm. Evidence for the algorithm, kept separate from inference: /usr/include/flint/fmpz.h:752-754 declares fmpz_is_probabprime_lucas, fmpz_is_probabprime_BPSW and fmpz_is_probabprime together, so BPSW and Lucas are the pieces flint provides -- but which of them the general entry point dispatches to for a given size should be read from flint's own documentation rather than taken from me, since the header only shows they are neighbours. Also worth fixing while someone is in there: the sentence 'there are no known numbers which are composite, and for which this function returns true, although it is expected that there are an infinite number of such primes' (isPrime-doc.m2:27-29) ends on 'such primes' where it means such composites. And the contrast with isPrime is undocumented and worth a line: isPrime goes to fmpz_is_prime, a proof, while this goes to fmpz_is_probabprime.

author: DanGrayson
title: degreeLength of basic engine rings?
note: All three of Dan's observations still hold, verified: degreeLength (ZZ/101) returns 0, degreesMonoid (ZZ/101) errors with 'no degreesMonoid for this ring', and degree 1_R returns {}. So a ring with no degrees monoid nonetheless reports a degree length of 0 and hands out empty degrees, which is the inconsistency he is pointing at -- he proposed that both should error instead. One comment, his own follow-up, and nothing since 2021-09-21. Sibling of #2237, filed the same day and also standing, and related to #3007 on degreeLength of a ZZ module.

author: antonleykin
title: Changing default values for options
note: The convenience method is unmet -- there is no setDefault anywhere in m2/ -- but the thread resolved the underlying need, which makes this a narrower row than it looks. mahrud gave two working recipes and Anton confirmed both: for a method defined with an option table, '(frame SVD)#0 = (frame SVD)#0 ++ {DivideConquer => true}'; for one defined with Options => true, the same against 'lookup(codim, Ideal)'; and more generally, install all methods of F on a new G and then 'symbol F <- G'. Anton's closing message is 'Both ways of setting the default options work', with a suggestion to discuss at M2internals whether a convenience method should be provided, perhaps with warnings. So what remains is a decision plus documentation, not a missing capability -- and mahrud twice noted that the frames and symbols mechanism these recipes rely on is itself undocumented, which is #2247 in this same batch. Dan's objection stands unaddressed too: a user changing a default breaks packages that rely on the documented one, and he recommended not pursuing it, pointing at Configuration options instead.

author: mahrud
title: Documentation for the interpreter
note: Unmet, and mahrud's claim about d/ is accurate on inspection: M2/Macaulay2/d/README is eight lines long, is a to-do list about mutexes and pthread_join rather than documentation, and was last touched in 2010. M2/Macaulay2/c/README is substantial at 377 lines but documents the translator rather than the language. His actual question -- what should be the preferred way to document the interpreter sources -- has had zero answers in four years. Worth knowing when this is picked up: partial material now exists outside the repository. The wiki pages drafted from this working copy (d-language.md, d-grammar.md, d-language-notes.md, grammar.md, simpledoc-grammar.md, all untracked in the repo root and uploaded by hand) cover the language's syntax for someone writing a parser, which is the 'no external way to learn the language' half of the complaint, though not the 'document the sources' half. Also relevant: #2240 in this same batch turns on the frames and symbols mechanism, which mahrud twice noted is undocumented -- a concrete instance of the cost this issue is about. #1668 is named in the body as the Core documentation gap.

author: mahrud
title: Profiling Computations
note: Partially implemented, and the part that is missing is the point of the issue. mahrud's own update says 'some of these are now added in #3431', and that is right: m2/computations.m2 now has ComputationCacheStats at :32, debug Computation at :114 toggling ComputationDebugLevel, status Computation at :117 returning the tally, and cacheHit Computation at :121-126 doing the counting. Missing: breakpoint Computation, and -- more importantly -- hash Computation. The existing code keys everything on 'hash C', the ordinary object hash of the computation container, whereas mahrud proposed a CONTENT hash, 'hash raw gens gb m', precisely so that the same Groebner basis computed twice from a redefined ring or ideal would be recognised as the same. Counting container hashes cannot detect that, which is the scenario the issue opens with. So the introspection scaffolding landed and the same-computation detection did not. The later comment about output formats -- pprof, the V8 table, flame graphs -- is a separate wish and untouched.

author: mahrud
title: Bug in nefGenerators weightedProjectiveSpace {1,1,2}
note: Reproduces exactly, including the asymmetry that is the actual puzzle: nefGenerators of weightedProjectiveSpace {2,1,1} and {1,2,1} both give matrix {{1}} while {1,1,2} gives matrix {{-1}}, and fromPicToCl {1,1,2} gives matrix {{-2}}. The thread is a genuine disagreement that ends in partial agreement worth recording: ggsmith's position is that for a singular variety Pic and Cl differ, the basis comes from a kernel of a ZZ-module map, and the signs carry no meaning -- he twice asked what a 'reasonable' basis would mean and asked for a reference, which mahrud supplied from Cox-Little-Schenck. But ggsmith's last message concedes something specific: the difference arises from the 'fromPic := matrix fromPicToCl X' line in (nefGenerators, NormalToricVariety), the nef cone is normally regarded as lying in the Picard group rather than the class group as the package's own documentation says, and 'I do regard this as a bug'. mahrud replied that he had not changed fromPicToCl and that his only change to nefGenerators, in 1cdeae8cf50, was to cache it. So there is maintainer agreement that the re-embedding is wrong, and nobody acted on it. mahrud's last lead, unfollowed, is that the divergence starts in cartierDivisorGroup where fromCDivToWDiv is cached.

author: pzinn
title: Use of == in Graphs
note: Reproduces: cartesianProduct(graph{{a,1}}, graph{{b,2}}) still errors with 'no method for binary operator == applied to objects: 1 (of class ZZ) == a (of class Symbol)'. The diagnosis in the thread is complete and unacted-on. pzinn identified that vertex labels can be anything while cartesianProduct compares them with ==, and suspected === is wanted and that other Graphs functions share the fault. Dan located it precisely: the illegal == is not in the vertex-set construction fchapoton suspected but in the edge comprehension, 'if (u_0 == v_0 and member(set {u_1, v_1}, edges H)) or (u_1 == v_1 and ...)'. He also offered a simplification, V := vertexSet G ** vertexSet H in place of toList(set ... ** set ...), and an aside that is arguably its own issue: it is strange that vertexSet returns a list rather than a set. Nothing was changed. Labelled package issue since Graphs is a distributed package and the fix is in it, not in Core.

author: mahrud
title: std::logic_error crash: inserted duplicate entry into a KD tree
note: Reproduces exactly and still aborts the process: 'R = ZZ/3[x,y,z]; isSupportedInZeroLocus(ideal vars R, HH_1 koszul vars R)' gives 'terminate called after throwing an instance of std::logic_error, what(): ERROR: Inserted duplicate entry into a KD tree' and dumps core on 1.26.06. As with #1984, this is a C++ exception escaping to std::terminate rather than being turned into a recoverable M2 error, so the interpreter never gets a chance to report it -- the same class of defect one library over, here in the KD tree used by the mathic/frobby side rather than in Monoid. mahrud's own observation that pruning the homology first avoids it is the workaround and also the clue: the duplicate entry presumably comes from unpruned generators that coincide.

author: mahrud
title: Add timelimit to capture with alarm
note: Unmet. capture still has no time limit: m2/examples.m2:144 excludes anything matching '(alarm|exec|exit|quit|restart|run)' from capture because 'these commands interrupt the interpreter', and :252 does 'alarm 0' to cancel alarms rather than to impose one, so there is nothing bounding a capture that never returns. mahrud's two asks -- a generous time limit on the M2 process that runs capture, and an alarm-based limit inside capture, possibly on a new thread -- are both unimplemented. Zero comments in four years. Note the diagnosis in the body is worth keeping: the jump in both build logs is between the third and fourth QthPower test, the test itself takes about 16s locally, and his guess is that finishing quickly needs more memory than the GitHub runners have -- so the failure is a hang under memory pressure rather than a genuinely slow test.

author: abhiramnatarajan
title: Matrix multiplication order reversed when elements are from Weyl algebra
note: Reproduces exactly. With D = makeWeylAlgebra QQ[x_11,x_12,x_21,x_22], a = x_11*dx_21 + x_12*dx_22 and b = x_22*dx_22 + 2, a*b ends in 3*x_12*dx_22 while (matrix{{a}}*matrix{{b}})_(0,0) ends in 2*x_12*dx_22 -- so matrix multiplication is still performed in the opposite algebra. What makes this row unusual for this corpus is that all four maintainers who spoke agreed it should change: Dan called it unnatural and said he and Mike had discussed fixing it, then 'I'm in favor of fixing it, since it's surprising'; Mike agreed but noted it is a larger change because it must stay compatible with Groebner bases; moorewf gave the argument in full -- since M2 already uses right modules and so represents linear maps as left multiplication, the multiplication should not be happening in the opposite ring -- and said he could not remember the reason for the current implementation. Against that, Anton told the reporter on Math StackExchange that it is intentional and the entries are to be read as coming from the opposite algebra. So the disagreement is between the thread and an off-tracker answer, and nothing was done. moorewf's second point is also untouched: the Kronecker product of matrices does not represent a tensor product of maps here in the way it would commutatively.

author: DanGrayson
title: Each package is allowed to document only its own symbols.
note: Unimplemented, and by inaction rather than decision. Dan split this out of #2263 to say 'We'll have to put that back to the way it was before'; mahrud replied 'This is both unnecessary and counterproductive'; there is no check in m2/document.m2 restricting a package to documenting its own symbols, and #2263 itself was closed by Dan the same week, with mahrud's last word there being that the PR fixed a bug in fixup and simplified help and should merge regardless of the disagreement. So the restriction was removed some versions before 2021, was never restored, and the row records a maintainer disagreement with one comment on each side and nothing since.

author: jkyang92
title: Mathicgb crash/assertion failure with Groebner bases
note: Cannot be observed on the reference build, and the reason matters more than the row. The assertion jkyang92 hit is MATHICGB_ASSERT(false) at e/mathicgb/mathicgb/F4MatrixBuilder2.cpp:133, in the else branch of a three-way dispatch over tasks[i].sPairPoly. That macro is live only under MATHICGB_DEBUG: stdinc.h:135 defines it as assert(X) inside '#ifdef MATHICGB_DEBUG' and :139 defines it as MATHICGB_ASSUME(X) otherwise -- which on GCC and Clang is ((void)0) at stdinc.h:82. (The __assume(X) form at :19, which would make this undefined behaviour, is the MSVC branch and does not apply.) So in a release build the check is a plain no-op: control falls out of the else branch, tasks[i] keeps both poly and sPairPoly set, and the state the author considered impossible is left in place rather than reported. Ran the attached reproducer (files/7480862/test2.m2.txt) five times on 1.26.06: all five completed cleanly, which is evidence about the assertion being compiled out, NOT about the bug being gone. jkyang92 saw it 'most of the time' from a source tree with DEBUG defined. Two connections: #1206, still open, is exactly this gating -- M2's configure stops defining NDEBUG under --enable-debug while mathicgb wants DEBUG defined -- so nobody gets these assertions by default; and #2162, where F4 'sometimes gives wrong results' on s390x, is the shape a suppressed check of this kind would produce. jkyang92 suspected a race or memory corruption and noted he is on amd64, unlike #2162.

author: mahrud
title: Twists of sheaves with higher Picard rank and arithmetic operations for sequences
note: Unmet. The ask has two halves and neither landed in Core: twists of sheaves by a multidegree on a variety of higher Picard rank, which mahrud notes the NormalToricVarieties package already fixes for its own varieties, and arithmetic on Sequences so that F(a+b) works the way {1,2} - 2*{4,5,6} does for lists. His follow-up points at m2/varieties.m2:179-202 as why cohomology of sheaves over a bigraded ring does not work. pzinn's 2021-11-24 comment adds a 2016 mailing-list exchange that is still the clearest statement of the underlying question -- Proj tests only isHomogeneous, so a ring with no grading passes; Dan's reply there was that single grading is expected but 'I'd be happier if the general case was handled with multi-Proj' and that he saw no reason to single out the first degree. So the row is really about whether Proj should be multigraded, and that has been open since 2016.

author: d-torrance
title: Illegal instruction making example results for FourTiTwo::toricGraverDegrees
note: Not ours to fix and not settled. The failure is 4ti2 itself dying with SIGILL -- 'Illegal instruction (core dumped)' from /usr/bin/4ti2-output --degrees -- during example generation for toricGraverDegrees, on an amd64 Ubuntu 22.04 PPA build, and Doug says so in the body: 'This is really a 4ti2 bug, but it affects Macaulay2.' He also could not reproduce it in an Ubuntu 22.04 chroot, and pinned the likely cause to 4ti2 1.6.9+ds-4 having just been uploaded to Debian unstable and synced to Ubuntu. An illegal instruction from a distro binary on amd64 usually means it was built with instructions the runner does not have, which is a packaging matter rather than an M2 one. Zero comments in four years. Two things would settle it: whether the current 4ti2 in Debian still does this, and whether M2 should report a signal from a helper program more clearly than 'error: 4ti2 returned an error'.

author: mahrud
title: Consistency of BettiTally ZZ with nonstandard heft vectors
note: Reproduces exactly. For K = koszul vars kk[x,y,z], peek B(10) gives keys (0,{0},-10) and (1,{1},-9), while peek betti(K ** S^{10}) gives (0,{-10},-10) and (1,{-9},-9): BettiTally ZZ shifts the weight and leaves the multidegree alone, so it does not 'mimic the corresponding operations on chain complexes' as its documentation claims. mahrud identified the one-line cause himself -- BettiTally ZZ := (C,n) -> applyKeys(C, (i,d,h) -> (i,d,h-n)) -- and his sharper point is the second example: with Heft => {2} the weight is twice the degree, so shifting only the weight makes the displayed table wrong, not merely inconsistent. Zero comments in four years. Same territory as #2159, triaged in batch 39 and also reproducing, where a null heft over a local ring zeroes the weights entirely.

author: mahrud
title: formation of tensor products of chain complexes
note: Reproduces, and the state has moved since filing, in the reporter's favour. formation(K ++ K) now works and returns directSum(Complex, Complex) -- when mahrud filed this, the Complexes package did not support formation at all and raised 'no method found for applying formation to ... (of class Complex)'. So direct sums of the new Complex type are covered. formation(K ** K) still returns null, which is the original complaint and is unchanged. Related: #2891 on components and formation of direct sums of matrices, #3971 on tensor of a list of lists.

author: d-torrance
title: out of memory capturing check(6, "K3Surfaces") on i386
note: Blanket-skipped here, so check proves nothing and the body was run directly: '-- no-check-flag' naming #2319 is a Debian patch in the installed K3Surfaces.m2. Extracted the flagged block -- a double loop over g from 3 to 12 and d from 3 to 5 calling K3(g,d,0) -- and ran it on amd64: it completes, reaching (g,d) = (12,5). That is the expected result and weak evidence, since the reported failure is out-of-memory on i386, where the 32-bit address space is the constraint rather than the algorithm; a row carrying build issue must not reach not-reproducible on an amd64 run. This is one of the four blanket-skipped rows flagged in the README, and it is the second of them to be triaged (after #2205, closed as obsolete when mips64el went); #2923 and #3238 remain.

author: mahrud
title: help ZZ after about and methods
note: Reproduces: after 'methods matrix', 'help 8' still gives "no previous 'about' response". mahrud's own analysis of why it is awkward is the state of things -- previousMethodsFound lives in code.m2 and is not visible where seeAbout reads lastabout, so numbering a methods listing and a numbering an about listing are two separate registers with no way to tell which was most recent. Zero comments in four years. Small and self-contained: the ask is that 'help n' resolve against whichever of the two listings came last.

author: lcrantonh
title: betti with degree 0 variables
note: Reproduces exactly. Over S = ZZ/101[x,y,Degrees => {{0},{1}}], peek betti(comodule ideal y) gives keys (0,{0},0) and (1,{1},0) -- the second entry has multidegree {1} but weight 0, which is why the table shows the row at -1 instead of at 1 -- while betti(M, Weights=>{1}) gives (1,{1},1) and displays correctly. Dan's diagnosis in the thread is right and is the connecting thread across three rows in this corpus: the ring has no heft vector, so the weight cannot be computed and defaults to 0. Same root as #2159 (heft null over a local ring, triaged batch 39, reproduces) and adjacent to #2303 (BettiTally ZZ shifts the weight but not the multidegree, triaged batch 42, reproduces). Whoever takes on heft defaults should take all three. Also #2338 in this batch is the same ring shape hitting poincare.

author: pzinn
title: relative paths in on-the-fly help
note: Reproduces per the record and unchanged in the source. The HREF in a package's 'Source code' paragraph is a path relative to the html output directory, which is right for html and wrong for the terminal: m2/format.m2 renders it as 'r | " (see " | x#0 | " )"' with x#0 used verbatim, and the comment two lines above says so -- 'x#0 is sometimes the relative path to the file, but not from the current directory'. Dan's suggested fix in the thread is still the obvious one: the toURL treatment that html HREF applies at m2/html.m2 should be mirrored for the net or info method, resolving relative to the current directory instead. One comment, his, in four years. Worth sequencing with the HTML documentation rewrite of Aug-Oct 2026 rather than against the current generator.

author: mahrud
title: poincare in presence of degree zero variables
note: Reproduces exactly: over kk[x,y, Degrees => {0,1}], poincare ideal(x,y) is 0 and poincare ideal(x+y^2) is 1-T^2. mahrud's suggestion is that it should error rather than return a meaningless answer, and zero comments followed in four years. Same ring shape as #2327 in this batch -- a degree-zero variable, hence no heft vector -- so the two are the same underlying gap surfacing in poincare and in betti respectively, and #909, which the body cross-references, is the older statement of it. Related: #732 on odd behaviour of gb and poincare.

author: mahrud
title: bug in Module / Module
note: Reproduces: with T = kk[z], module ideal z^2 divided by comodule ideal z^2 returns cokernel matrix {{1}} rather than erroring. mahrud's argument is that this cannot be meant: N is not a submodule of M, they are not submodules of a common module so (M+N)/N does not rescue it, and the answer is wrong even as vector spaces since M is spanned by z^2, z^3, ... and N by 1, z. Eleven comments -- the longest thread in this batch -- and nothing changed.

author: mahrud
title: documentation of hooks
note: Unmet: m2/help.m2 makes no mention of hooks, so a method's available strategies are still invisible from 'help' and discoverable only by calling 'hooks' directly, which is what mahrud demonstrates in the body. Zero comments in four years. He is right that the ingredients exist -- hooks(saturate, Ideal, Ideal) already returns the strategy list, and his one-liner extracts just the names -- so this is a small addition to the help renderer rather than new machinery. Related: #1626 on making code work on more types of hooks, #1153 on parallel hooks.

author: d-torrance
title: Error: not divisible in FreeAlgebra.create unit test
note: Untestable here -- unit tests are not shipped in the reference build -- but the source tells a useful story. The failure was 'Error: not divisible' then EXPECT_TRUE(false) at NCGroebnerTest.cpp:270. That line has moved (the file was reorganised in 2026, including 8a667ffd05 moving monomial code to e/monomial), but the check is still the first block of TEST(FreeAlgebra, create) at :238-244: 'if (degreeRing(1) == nullptr or error()) { std::cout << "Error: " << error_message(); EXPECT_TRUE(false); }'. Note what that conflates: error() reads a GLOBAL error flag, so this fires either because degreeRing(1) failed or because anything earlier in the process left an error set. 'not divisible' is not a message degreeRing would produce, so the likeliest reading is a stale error from earlier work being reported here -- which would explain why only this one of the five FreeAlgebra tests failed while the other four passed in the same run. Doug asked whether it relates to #2324; unexamined. Zero comments in four years.

author: mahrud
title: `when .. is .. else ..` for top-level switch statements
note: Stands. Unmet: there is no top-level 'when ... is ... else' and 'when' is not a keyword at the M2 prompt, though it is one in the d language. ASKED AND ANSWERED: Doug was leaning wontfix and asked for the case; on being shown that this is a general switch-statement request rather than a request to mimic d's when, he said keep it. That distinction is the whole thread and it is easy to miss, because it lives in the fourth of five comments. mahrud's opening invokes d's when AND asks for inheritance-awareness, so Dan read it as type dispatch and replied 'dispatching via method functions is probably enough for all practical purposes'; two comments later Dan says so explicitly -- 'you mentioned inheritance in your original post, and invoked the "when" statement in the D language, so I inferred you intended this to be used for type dispatch' -- and mahrud answers 'No I meant a general switch statement', with an example switching on opts.Strategy, a Symbol rather than a type. So Dan's objection was withdrawn by clarification, not sustained, and his LAST word is a build recipe rather than a refusal: add the keywords with suitable parsing precedence, add an item to the union type Code and one to ParseTree, and follow ifCode and IfThenElse. That recipe is the durable output of the thread and is why the row is worth keeping -- it makes this a specified starter project for someone learning the interpreter, which is the gap #2247 is about. Arguments the other way, recorded so they are not re-derived: it is convenience rather than capability, since Core already switches on Strategy symbols twelve times with plain 'if opts.Strategy === Foo then' and type dispatch already supplies the inheritance mahrud wanted; the cost is a language change touching parser, converter and evaluator; and #1978 is the same shape of stalled parser-convenience request, which Dan resisted on the ground that it makes the language more complicated. No retitle proposed: the title does say 'switch statements', so it is the body's framing that misleads, not the title.

author: mahrud
title: Base change
note: Reproduces on all three reported lines, and this row already carries a comment from this project posted 2026-08-08 under the marker bug-triage:bugs/dan/1-newRing, so no further comment is proposed. Verified: ZZ[a,b] ** QQ gives QQ[a..b]; ZZ/101[c,d] ** QQ errors; ZZ[e,f] ** ZZ/101 errors; and the worse symptom that comment identified is live too -- with k = ZZ/5 and R = k[u,v], k ** R errors although newring.m2 opens tensor(Ring,Ring) with 'if R === (try coefficientRing S) then return S'. The cause in that comment is dispatch rather than a missing case: QuotientRing ** PolynomialRing at newring.m2:62 is more specific, so any QuotientRing coefficient ring routes to :68 whose first line is coefficientRing R, and coefficientRing (ZZ/101) is the 'no coefficient ring present' error. The documentation-page half of the ask is also unmet, and the comment records that k (monoid R) is the working spelling for polynomial rings, documented at doc_rings.m2:253 and used at about fifteen sites, dropping relations for quotients. Removing the 'bug' label as bookkeeping now that the type is Bug.

author: d-torrance
title: Hooks and recursion depth

His 2022-09-06 comment is the live ask and it is addressed to Dan: the remaining cost is in the interpreter's method-call evaluation, which he calls impenetrable, and he asks specifically for evaluate.d and actors5.d to be commented, noting that a lot of the existing comments are incorrect because they reference features that no longer exist. author: mahrud
title: hypertext objects in documentation headlines
note: Reproduces, and the open question our own comment posed now has an answer. The comment posted 2026-08-06 under the marker bug-triage:bugs/dan/1-doc-headlines asked how linSpace acquired a hypertext headline given that document requires a string at document.m2:601-604 and SimpleDoc enforces the same through singleString at SimpleDoc.m2:81. The source is Polyhedra/documentation/documentation.m2:102-103, which has 'Headline' followed by 'Deprecated version of @TO "linealitySpace"@'. So singleString cannot catch it: @TO "..."@ IS a single string at parse time and only becomes a Hypertext object when the doc string is processed, which means the check is at the wrong level rather than being bypassed. Offered as a reading rather than a proof -- I did not trace the processing. The design question the comment raised stands unanswered: this issue asks for non-strings in headlines to error, while bugs/dan/1-doc-headlines asks for headlines to support everything including TeX, and the asymmetry is that allowing markup obliges every consumer of headlines to render it, including terminal help, about results, info files and package tables of contents.

author: mahrud
title: Bug in multigraded Ext computation
note: Reproduces on a stock build now, and that is the finding -- it did not when ggsmith tried in 2022. Verified: HH^1(X, OO_X(-2,2)) is QQ^6 and Ext^1(OO_X, OO_X(-2,2)) is QQ^0 on X = toricProjectiveSpace 1 ** toricProjectiveSpace 2, so they disagree where Hartshorne III 6.3 says they must agree, and mahrud's belief that QQ^6 is right is consistent with HH being the one computed correctly. In 2022 ggsmith got 'expected sheaves on a projective variety' and reasonably asked whether mahrud had altered his local copy. What changed: the sheaf code moved out of Core into the Varieties package, and Ext(ZZ, CoherentSheaf, CoherentSheaf) now lives at Varieties.m2:758-765 with NO projective-variety guard -- that check survives only in Varieties/SheafComplexes.m2 at :159, :186 and :210. So the input that used to be refused is now accepted and answered wrongly, which is a regression in safety rather than in arithmetic. ggsmith's substantive point is untouched and explains the wrong answer: the algorithm assumes sheaves represented by ZZ-graded modules over a standard graded polynomial ring, and the implementation computes via basis(0, E) on G(>=0), which is exactly that assumption. He also said he had once worked out the relevant generalizations.

author: DanGrayson
title: `exportFrom` documentation misfeature
note: Unresolved, and it is a design disagreement about symbol ownership rather than a bug with a fix. Dan's position: a symbol should belong to one package, exportFrom breaks that, M2 then picks up the other package's example code for the symbol and reruns it -- which can fail because not all of that package's symbols are present -- and he floated removing exportFrom altogether. mahrud's position: exportFrom means the symbol is now part of this package, he uses it, and the right fix is a check that it was not already exported elsewhere. Dan's objection to that is concrete and unanswered: verifying no other package exported it would mean loading every package. His own last proposal, also unacted-on, is to add a field to symbol closures recording which package a symbol was exported from, so double export could be prevented cheaply. Greg Smith's failing files, which Dan offered to forward, never reached the thread, so the demonstration mahrud asked for twice is still missing. author: pzinn
title: coefficients in iterated rings
note: Reproduces exactly: over R = QQ[x], S = R[y], coefficients(x+y, Monomials=>{x,y}) returns monomials matrix {{x, y}} and coefficients matrix {{x}, {1}}, whose product is matrix {{y+x^2}} rather than x+y -- so the documented identity between the two outputs fails. Mike's reply is unambiguous, 'This is definitely a bug!', and he sketched the fix: if Variables or Monomials is given, their support should be variables of the outer ring and otherwise an error, since flattening the ring implicitly is not a good idea. pzinn agreed flattening is wrong and offered the alternative -- normalise the monomial so the constant comes out into the coefficient, giving {| 1 y |, | x |; | 1 |}, which at least satisfies the identity. Neither was implemented. Two later observations widen it rather than resolve it: mahrud's 2024-08-05 note that f // m already gives a correct factorisation over the tower ring, so the information is obtainable; and pzinn's 2024-09-19 example showing Variables is worse still, since coefficients(F, Variables=>{a,b,c}) and coefficients(F, Variables=>{a,b,c,d,e,f}) give different and both odd answers on the documentation's own example. Labels 'seeking a volunteer' and 'good beginners' project' left in place, though Mike calling it a bug he is unsure how to handle sits oddly with the second.

author: mahrud
title: O(1) list and sequence operations
note: Unimplemented, and it is the root of #2562 in this same batch. mahrud's point is that toList toSequence toList(10^8:0) costs about 5x what constructing (10^8:0) does, and that operations of this shape should be O(1). Nothing has been done: zero comments in three years. Mike's aside on #2562 -- 'maybe it would be nice if 1..10^7 would not expand before the loop?' -- is the same request from the other end, and measuring #2562 showed what the expansion costs: a single scan(0..10^7, i -> ()) takes RSS from 125 MB to 1,091 MB. Related, as the body says: #1608, #1904 (iterators, now implemented, closed in batch 35) and #1978.

author: mahrud
title: Memory leak in creating a sequence
note: Measured, and it is bounded growth rather than a leak. Running f = () -> (scan(0..10^7, i -> ());) repeatedly with collectGarbage between: RSS goes 124,788 kB at baseline, then 1,090,940 after the first call, 1,650,364 after the second, 1,655,464 after the third and 1,655,464 after the fourth -- so it grows for two calls and then plateaus. That matches Mike's report ('uses consistently 1.37 GB') and Dan's explanation: the value of a top-level expression is retained even with a trailing semicolon, each element carries type and gmp overhead, and libgc tracks every allocation, so 10^7 elements is on the order of a gigabyte. mahrud's counter -- that the value is one object -- is answered by the fact that the object is a sequence of 10^7 pointers. His transcript showing 6.4 GB to 8.5 GB used over three calls is consistent with the first-two-calls growth above and he stopped there. So the row is not a leak; what is real is the cost of materialising 0..10^7 at all, which is #2561, kept open. Left open rather than proposed for closing since the verdict is mine and the reporter's underlying complaint has a live home.

author: mahrud
title: Bug in pruning map over ZZ with torsion
note: Reproduces: with N = prune coker matrix{{2,-1},{-1,2},{-1,-1}} and f = inverse N.cache.pruningMap, f is matrix {{-1,-2,0},{1,1,1}} while map(target f, source f, matrix f) is matrix {{-1,1,0},{1,1,1}}, and f == g is false. The two agree as maps of ZZ-modules but not as matrices, so mahrud's expectation that f == map(target f, source f, matrix f) should always hold fails. Dan confirmed it in one line and named a likely cause that nobody followed up: 'Perhaps inverse is not reducing the matrix it finds modulo the relations in the target.' The secondary transcript in the body is the sharper reproduction -- over R = ZZ/3, map(R, raw matrix{{2}}) and matrix(R, {{2}}) compare with 'error: expected same ring' while ring m === ring n is true -- so the ring check is looking at something other than the ring.

title: Spurious layers when debugging

Related: #1928, closed in batch 35 after mahrud's own breakpoint keyword landed, and #2569 in this batch, which is the same layers seen through locate and code rather than through the debugger.

author: mahrud
title: locate and code for functions involving options, caching, or @@ are useless
note: Reproduces and is the longest thread in this batch at 22 comments, all mahrud's own escalation with no maintainer reply. The complaint is that locate and code report the generic wrapper rather than the definition: locate(net, Variety) points at classes.m2:90, the definition of Function @@ Function, rather than at varieties.m2 where net Variety is defined; code(codim, ProjectiveVariety) shows option.m2's 'uncurry(f, override (opts,args))' with the real source relegated to a '-- function f:' section; and code(poincare, MonomialIdeal) shows the body of cacheValue. author: mahrud
title: DegreeLift doesn't work for maps of multigraded rings
note: Reproduces exactly: with A = QQ[a,b, Degrees => {{1,0},{0,1}}] and B = newRing(A, Degrees => reverse degrees A), isHomogeneous f1 is true while isHomogeneous inverse f1 is false, and supplying DegreeLift => reverse as well gives the same -- f2 homogeneous, inverse f2 not. So DegreeLift does not preserve homogeneity under inverse, which mahrud presumes is the main point of it. Third row in this corpus on the same mechanism: #1919 (the degree map lives in the cache and so plays no part in ring map equality, batch 35, stands) and #2368 (map of multigraded modules drops degrees, batch 44, reproduces, where Dan's advice was to supply a DegreeMap and mahrud's answer was that its multigraded use is hard and poorly documented). This row is the evidence for that answer.

author: mahrud
title: List ^ ZZ for permutations

Worth noting for whoever picks it up that the semantics need settling first, since w^2 for w = {2,0,1} meaning w_w is composition of the permutation with itself, which only makes sense for lists that are permutations of 0..n-1, and List ^ ZZ is currently free for other meanings -- so this is a notation-reservation question as much as an implementation one.
